messages.content: i can compute the transform of a rect but i don't *get* what the integral is doing

Think of e^(-j2πft) as a **probe spinning at frequency f**.

1. Multiply your signal by the probe.
2. If x(t) contains a component at exactly f, that component and the probe spin together → their product stops rotating and **adds up** over time.
3. Every other frequency keeps rotating relative to the probe and **averages to zero**.

So X(f) is "how much of x(t) survives when you look at it through a lens spinning at f". The rect pulse is short, so many probe speeds partially survive → wide sinc.
ok that actually clicks. so a longer pulse = narrower sinc because only probes really close to 0 survive?

Yes — that's the scaling property in one sentence. Over a long pulse, even a slightly-off probe has time to drift a full cycle and cancel, so only f ≈ 0 survives. Short pulse → not enough time to cancel → broad spectrum. Same reason a short click sounds "broadband".
why do we notch at 50 Hz and not 60 like in the matlab example online?

Mains frequency depends on the grid: **50 Hz in Europe** (Italy included), 60 Hz in North America. The tutorial you found was US-based. On page 2 your notes show the sharp peak at 50 Hz in the recorded ECG spectrum — that's what you filter.

cards.q: Rect pulse of width T transforms to?
cards.a: T sinc(fT). Narrower pulse -> wider spectrum.

cards.q: Effect of a time shift t0 on X(f)?
cards.a: Multiplies X(f) by e^(-j2 pi f t0): only phase changes, magnitude is unchanged.
